title: An art exhibition inspired by the age of spices

paragraphs.text: 'Treasure Ships' was a recent art exhibition at the Art Gallery of South Australia. Its purpose was to present the story of east-west artistic exchange in the era 1500-1800. This is the era known as the 'age of spices'. The exhibition included objects ranging from paintings and decorative arts to manuscripts and articles taken from wrecked ships. These objects revealed how the international trade in spices and other exotic commodities inspired dialogue between Asian and European artists.

Europe's infatuation with spices like pepper, nutmeg and cloves has often been explained as a belief that spices were able to preserve cooked foods in the days before the invention of refrigeration. It is true that some spices do contain microbiological elements that may significantly hinder decay but there were other important reasons for their immense value, such as their medicinal uses. Nutmeg and cinnamon were considered valuable in treating ailments ranging from vomiting to depression. Whatever the reasons, these spices became condiments of luxury and status that were keenly sought, often at great expense to human lives and resources, from unknown distant lands.

Portugal remapped the West's view of the world and opened the era of direct cultural exchange with the East when, in 1498, the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama became the first European to reach India via the Cape of Good Hope at the bottom of Africa. He and his small fleet of ships landed in Kerala on the west coast of the Indian subcontinent. They found there a prosperous, far-reaching network of international trade that utilised the annual monsoon winds to aid trade. Within a decade, the Portuguese had seized control of the Indian Ocean spice trade.

New forms of art inevitably arose as a result of the movement of people and media along Portuguese spice trading routes. Due to its potential for exceptionally fine carving, elephant ivory was favoured for the creation of Christian images. The seemingly inexhaustible availability of tropical pearls inspired European fashion trends throughout the 1500s.

In 1602, the Dutch United East India Company was established. This company heralded the beginning of the modern age of the multinational company and had the first internationally recognised commercial trademark. Over the next 200 years, the company maintained a global monopoly in the sale of spices. At the beginning of the 19th century, Europe had not yet embarked on the industrial revolution, and the two most eagerly sought after manufactured products for trade were Indian printed textiles and high-fired East Asian ceramics, which were far superior to any comparable item being made in Europe.

Over the centuries, the spice trade and the increased engagement with Asia inspired curiosity and investigation. In the 1800s, art gained a new significance as artists sought to render visible the marvels of the largely unknown parts of the world. Improved printing techniques stimulated a demand for lavishly illustrated travel books and grand sea atlases, which presented the latest discoveries to an eager reading public.

An early example of the European fascination with eastern exotica was typified in the 1600s by 'tulip mania' which gripped the Netherlands. At this time, the tulip, an introduced flower, became so popular that its value increased and collectors paid fantastic sums to obtain rare tulip plants. At one point, a particular tulip type could sell for the equivalent of the amount of money it would have taken the average Dutch bricklayer fifteen years to earn. Tulips became an enduring subject of paintings in Europe as they had long been in Turkey, where they originated.

In Southeast Asia, the age of spices was a period of extraordinary cultural growth and development. The Javanese and Malay sultanates nurtured visual, performing and literary arts that reflected the coastal surroundings. The islands of Java, Sumatra and Borneo were covered in dense jungle so rivers were the main means of transport. Inland commodities, including spices and other forest products, were traded for porcelain and other manufactured goods. However, today the importance of the ports such as Bandar Melaka, Banten and Bandar Aceh is easily overlooked as most of their buildings, even Melaka's grand palace, were constructed in wood and other temporary materials that have long since vanished. The islands of Java, Sumatra and Borneo held ceremonial gatherings of massive flotillas of boats. These became occasions of state theatre and were depicted in textiles showing fantastic ships, whose imagery simultaneously references social order on land and actual sea-going vessels.

The discovery by Europeans of the land that was later called Australia was a by-product of the spice age. This land was a mystery to them as can be witnessed by the variety of names given to it, for example: Beach, Greater Java, Southern India and Terra Incognita (unknown land). These names clearly reflect European confusion regarding the location of the land and its size. Despite this, a Portuguese cartographer was so confident of the eventual European settlement of the country that he designed its national coat of arms, which featured a dove with a branch of greenery in its beak.

It was appropriate that this exhibition, of artistic exchange between the east and west, was held in Adelaide as this is the only Australian city founded on the vision of a Eurasian – Colonel William Light, a British Surveyor-General whose mother was Malay and father was English.
